title: Kanchenjunga as guardian in Lepcha and Sikkimese belief
meta_description: How Lepcha and Sikkimese Buddhist belief treat Kanchenjunga as guardian: creation stories, the Kabi oath, Pang Lhabsol, and how to visit with respect.
summary: To the people of Sikkim, Kanchenjunga is not only the world's third-highest mountain, at 8,586 m. Lepcha elders tell that the first people were shaped from its snows, and Sikkimese Buddhists honour it as Dzö-nga, the protector deity of the land, at the Pang Lhabsol festival each late summer. This is a guide to that belief, told as belief.
key_takeaways: In Lepcha tradition the creator mother Itbu-moo shaped the first man and woman from the snows of Kanchenjunga, which the Lepchas call Kongchen Konglo.
Sikkimese Buddhists honour the mountain as Dzö-nga, a protector deity, and the Pang Lhabsol festival in August or September is devoted to it.
The oath of brotherhood between the Lepcha Thekong Tek and the Bhutia Khye Bumsa at Kabi Lungchok called the mountain as witness.
The 1955 first ascent stopped short of the true summit out of respect, and Sikkim treats the peak and its lakes as sacred ground.

sections.heading: A mountain with a name and a role
paras: Kanchenjunga rises to 8,586 m on the border of Sikkim and Nepal, the third-highest mountain on earth. From Darjeeling, Pelling, Yuksom and Gangtok it fills the northern sky on clear mornings, and for most visitors that view is the reason to come. For the people who have lived beneath it for centuries, the mountain is something more: a presence that protects the land, watches over oaths and receives the dead.

The name most travellers use comes from Tibetan, Kang-chen-dzö-nga, usually translated as the five treasures of the great snow. The five treasures are traditionally linked to the mountain's five summits and listed as stores of gold, silver, precious stones, grain and holy books, though versions differ. What follows is belief and tradition as the communities themselves tell it. We describe it, we do not test it, and we have left out stories we could not trace to a reliable source.

sections.heading: Lepcha belief: born of the snows
paras: The Lepchas are regarded as Sikkim's first people. They call themselves Mutanchi Rongkup, often rendered as the beloved children of the mother creator, and their name for the land is Mayel Lyang. In their language the mountain is Kongchen Konglo.

Lepcha elders tell that Itbu-moo, the creator mother, shaped the first man, Fudongthing, and the first woman, Nazaong Nyu, from the pure snows of Kongchen Konglo. The mountain is therefore not only a guardian but an origin: the place the people came from. Lepcha clans traditionally trace their ancestry to particular peaks, lakes and rivers in its shadow, and many rituals turn toward it. Lepcha priests, the bongthing and the mun, are said to guide the souls of the dead along an ancestral path back toward the mountain.

The heart of Lepcha country today is Dzongu, a reserve of valleys between the Teesta and Kanchenjunga's slopes, set aside for the Lepchas in the time of the Chogyals. Outsiders need a permit to enter, and the villages still speak Lepcha at home. Dzongu is in North Sikkim, where roads have had long closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Two traditions side by side
paras: Lepcha and Buddhist beliefs about the mountain grew up together in Sikkim and overlap in many places. This table sets out the main threads as they are usually told.

sections.heading: Dzö-nga, the protector of a hidden land
paras: In Sikkimese Buddhist tradition the country is a beyul, a hidden valley blessed by Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava, the teacher credited with bringing Buddhism to the Himalaya in the 8th century. The story told in Sikkim is that he bound the powerful spirits of the land and made them protectors of the Dharma, and the greatest of these is the spirit of the mountain, Dzö-nga. He is pictured as a warrior deity riding a white snow lion, attended by a commander called Yabdu.

Lhatsun Chenpo and two other lamas came over the passes in the 17th century, and in 1642, at Norbugang near Yuksom, they consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim. Yuksom sits directly below the mountain, and the trail to Dzongri and Goecha La still starts there. Monasteries across West Sikkim, Pemayangtse and Tashiding among them, face toward Kanchenjunga, and lamas speak of the peaks, lakes and caves of the region as places of power.

sections.heading: The oath at Kabi and the Pang Lhabsol festival
paras: Sikkim's own history ties the two peoples together under the mountain's gaze. Tradition tells that in the 13th century Khye Bumsa, a prince from eastern Tibet, crossed into Sikkim to seek the blessing of the Lepcha holy man Thekong Tek. At Kabi Lungchok, north of Gangtok, the two swore an oath of blood brotherhood, calling on the mountain gods and Kanchenjunga as witnesses that Lepchas and Bhutias would be one family. Stones mark the site, and statues of the two men stand there today.

Pang Lhabsol, roughly the worship of the witness gods, keeps that oath alive. The festival is credited to the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, and falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, in late August or September. Its centrepiece is the pangtoed cham, a warrior dance by men in helmets and armour with swords and shields, alongside a masked figure of the mountain deity on a snow lion. The best-known celebrations are at the Tsuklakhang in Gangtok and at Ravangla in South Sikkim. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A summit left untouched
paras: The belief has reached the climbing world too. When a British expedition led by Charles Evans made the first ascent of Kanchenjunga in 1955, Joe Brown and George Band stopped a short distance below the very top, on 25 May, honouring an undertaking that the summit itself would not be trodden, out of respect for the mountain's sacred status in Sikkim. Many later climbers on the Nepal side have kept the same custom.

Within Sikkim, the mountain and the land around it are protected. Khangchendzonga National Park became India's first mixed natural and cultural World Heritage Site in 2016, recognised partly for the sacred meaning of its peaks, lakes and caves to Lepcha and Buddhist communities. Summit expeditions are not permitted from the Sikkim side; trekkers go as far as Goecha La on a permit, and rules change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Where to see the mountain and its places
paras: The mountain shows itself most reliably from October to early December and in March and April, and nearly always in the first hours after dawn; by late morning cloud usually builds over the peaks. In the monsoon, from June to September, you may not see it for weeks, which is when Pang Lhabsol falls, so the festival and the view rarely come together.

In West Sikkim, Pelling, at about 2,100 m, faces the range head-on, and Pemayangtse monastery above the town looks straight at it. Yuksom, the old first capital, lies at its foot, with Norbugang and its coronation throne a short walk from the bazaar. Tashiding monastery, on a hilltop between two rivers, is among the most sacred sites in Sikkim and holds the Bumchu ceremony each year. Ravangla, in South Sikkim, has the Pang Lhabsol dances and a long view north on clear mornings.

From Gangtok the range rises above the ridges to the north-west; on a clear day the view from the town's high points takes in Kanchenjunga and its neighbours. Kabi Lungchok, the site of the oath, is about 17 km north of Gangtok on the road toward Mangan.

sections.heading: Visiting with respect
paras: Travellers meet this belief in small ways: a prayer flag line facing the peaks at Pelling, a chorten on a pass, a quiet stretch at a sacred lake. Khecheopalri Lake, below Pelling, is one of the holiest, and the local story says birds keep its surface clear of fallen leaves. A few simple habits go a long way.
list: Walk clockwise around chortens, mani walls and monasteries.
Do not swim, wash or throw anything into sacred lakes such as Khecheopalri.
Ask before photographing rituals, monks or masked dancers.
Never step over or sit on prayer flags, offerings or stones at a shrine.
In Dzongu, follow your homestay host's lead on where visitors may go.

faqs.q: Why is Kanchenjunga sacred in Sikkim?
faqs.a: For the Lepchas, Sikkim's first people, the mountain is the origin of humankind: elders tell that the creator mother Itbu-moo shaped the first man and woman from its snows. For Sikkimese Buddhists it is Dzö-nga, a protector deity bound to defend the land and its faith. Both traditions treat it as the guardian of Sikkim and a witness to sacred oaths.

faqs.q: What does the name Kanchenjunga mean?
faqs.a: The name comes from Tibetan, Kang-chen-dzö-nga, usually translated as the five treasures of the great snow. The five treasures are traditionally linked to the mountain's five summits and described as stores of gold, silver, precious stones, grain and holy books, though versions vary. The Lepchas have their own name for the mountain, Kongchen Konglo.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol and where can I see it?
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, usually in late August or September. The best-known celebrations are at the Tsuklakhang royal chapel in Gangtok and at Ravangla in South Sikkim, with the pangtoed warrior dance. Dates follow the lunar calendar and it is late monsoon, so check current status before you travel and expect rain.

faqs.q: Did the first climbers reach the summit of Kanchenjunga?
faqs.a: Joe Brown and George Band of the 1955 British expedition climbed to within a short distance of the top on 25 May 1955 and deliberately stopped short of the highest point, honouring an undertaking made out of respect for the mountain's sacredness in Sikkim. Many later climbers on the Nepal side have kept that custom. Summit expeditions are not permitted from the Sikkim side.

faqs.q: Can visitors go to Dzongu to learn about Lepcha culture?
faqs.a: Yes, with a permit. Dzongu is a protected Lepcha reserve in North Sikkim; Indian visitors get a special permit, usually arranged in Mangan or through a Dzongu homestay, and rules for foreign visitors are stricter. Homestays offer Lepcha food and village walks. North Sikkim roads have had long closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, so check current status before you travel.
